name: Monteggia fracture-dislocation
aliases: proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation

reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: A fracture of the proximal ulna combined with dislocation of the radial head
The radial head typically dislocates in the direction the apex of the ulnar fracture points, described by the Bado classification (anterior, posterior, lateral, or both-bone types)
A useful memory aid contrasts Monteggia (ulna fracture with radial head dislocation) against Galeazzi (radius fracture with distal radioulnar joint injury)
The radiocapitellar line should pass through the centre of the capitellum on every view; if it does not, the radial head is dislocated
In adults the ulna requires open reduction and internal fixation restoring its length and bow, which usually reduces the radial head
A missed radial head dislocation is a common and serious error, especially in children
Posterior interosseous nerve palsy may accompany the injury, particularly in lateral and posterior patterns
reference.pathophysiology: A fracture of the proximal ulna alters the length and alignment of the bone. Because the radius and ulna are coupled proximally through the annular ligament and the proximal radioulnar joint, ulnar deformity displaces the radial head from its articulation with the capitellum. Restoring anatomical ulnar length and curvature is therefore essential, as residual ulnar malalignment leaves the radial head subluxed or dislocated. The dislocating radial head can also stretch or injure the posterior interosseous nerve as it passes around the radial neck.
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the elbow and the entire forearm
Confirmation that the radiocapitellar line intersects the capitellum on all views
Contralateral comparison radiographs, particularly in children
CT for complex or comminuted proximal ulna fractures
Careful documentation of posterior interosseous nerve function
redFlags: Missed dislocation of the radial head
reference.prognosis: Anatomical restoration of ulnar length and alignment usually re-establishes radiocapitellar congruity with a good outcome; missed dislocation, ulnar malreduction or nerve injury worsen the result.
pitfalls: Failing to check the radiocapitellar line and thereby missing the radial head dislocation
Inadequate restoration of ulnar length and bow, leaving the radial head subluxed
Overlooking a posterior interosseous nerve palsy
Not imaging the full forearm including the elbow
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
